title: Reciprocity
description: The hardwired psychological urge to return a favor when someone gives you something.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: When someone gives you something or does you a favor, you feel an automatic, built-in urge to give something back. The scales feel unbalanced until you return the gesture.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Human survival historically relied on sharing resources. We are wired to avoid the social stigma of being a 'taker'. When we receive unearned value, our brain registers uncomfortable social debt.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: Business: A software company giving a free 30-day trial without asking for a credit card.
Sales: A car dealer buying you a coffee or lunch while you 'think it over'.
Workplace: A coworker covering your shift, expecting you to cover theirs later.
Daily Life: Receiving a holiday card from someone and instantly feeling you must send one back.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Person A: 'Hey, I brought you that coffee you like from the place down the street!'
Person B: 'Oh wow, thank you so much! I owe you one.'
Person A (an hour later): 'Hey, actually, could you help me finish this report? I am swamped.'
Person B: '...Yeah, sure, no problem.' (Thinks: I literally just drank the coffee he bought me, I can't say no.)

sections.title: Pattern Recognition
content: Unsolicited gifts given right before a pitch.
People doing small favors that were never asked for.
Extreme 'generosity' from a stranger who quickly transitions into an 'ask'.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Providing genuine, high-quality value upfront with no hidden agenda, allowing the recipient to freely choose whether or not to engage with you later. E.g., sharing knowledge freely to build a real relationship.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Creating artificial debt by forcing a 'gift' on someone (like putting a flower in their hand on the street) and then demanding a donation, weaponizing their guilt.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A favor that feels forced, overly intimate, or wildly disproportionate.
An immediate, specific request directly following a gift.
The person verbally brings up the favor they did for you to pressure you.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Mentally reframe the 'gift' as a 'transactional sales tactic'.
Decline unnecessary favors from people you do not fully trust.
Delay your response. Let the initial emotional guilt fade before answering their request.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Giving something back immediately out of sheer discomfort.
Assuming all favors are done out of pure kindness.
Feeling indebted for a gift they didn't even ask for or want.

sections.title: Case Study
sections.content: A charity sends personalized return address labels in the mail alongside a donation request. The cost of the labels is pennies. However, because the recipient has 'received' something tangible, the psychological urge to reciprocate drives the donation rate up by double digits compared to sending a standard letter alone.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: 1. Unsolicited gifts create powerful social debt.
2. Free value is rarely completely free.
3. You are under no obligation to repay a gift you never asked for.
4. The best defense is mental separation: evaluate the request completely independently of the gift.
